questions.question: The chapter's epigraph argues against a particular position about two-phase commit. Who wrote it, and where?

options.text: James Corbett et al., Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012)
Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter, Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery (1983)
Jim Gray, The Transaction Concept (1981)
Eric Brewer, Towards Robust Distributed Systems (2000)

questions.explanation: The position it argues against is that you should code around the absence of transactions rather than pay for them.

questions.question: Which things does the chapter list as going wrong 'in the harsh reality of data systems'? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The database software or hardware may fail at any time, including in the middle of a write operation; and the application may crash at any time, including halfway through a series of operations
Interruptions in the network can unexpectedly cut off the application from the database, or one database node from another
Several clients may write at the same time, overwriting each other's changes; and a client may read data that doesn't make sense because it has only partially been updated
Race conditions between clients can cause surprising bugs

questions.explanation: Six things in all. Ensuring these don't cause catastrophic failure requires a lot of work — and a lot of testing.

questions.question: Give the chapter's definition of a transaction.

options.text: A way for an application to group several reads and writes together into a logical unit: conceptually all the reads and writes are executed as one operation, and the entire transaction either succeeds (commit) or fails (abort, rollback) — so there is no such thing as a partial failure
A single atomic write to one object
A lock held for the duration of a session
A durable log entry describing a change

questions.explanation: No partial failure is the property that everything else in the chapter builds on.

questions.question: 'Transactions are not a law of nature.' What were they created for?

options.text: To simplify the programming model for applications accessing a database: with transactions the application is free to ignore certain potential error scenarios and concurrency issues because the database takes care of them instead — the chapter calls these safety guarantees
To improve write throughput
To enable distributed consensus
To satisfy regulatory audit requirements

questions.explanation: Programmer convenience, purchased from the database at a cost.

questions.question: Does the chapter claim every application needs transactions?

options.text: No — not every application needs them, and sometimes there are advantages to weakening transactional guarantees or abandoning them entirely, for example to achieve higher performance or higher availability
Yes — every application that writes data needs them
Only applications handling financial data need them
Only distributed applications need them

questions.explanation: To decide, you need to understand exactly what safety guarantees transactions can provide and what costs are associated with them — and although transactions seem straightforward at first glance, there are many subtle but important details.

questions.question: Where does today's transaction style come from, and how much has it changed?

options.text: Most databases follow the style introduced in 1975 by IBM System R, the first SQL database; although some implementation details have changed, the general idea has remained largely the same for 40 years — the transaction support in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server is uncannily similar to that of System R
From Oracle in 1985, and it has been rewritten several times since
From the SQL standard in 1992, replacing earlier incompatible designs
From the ACID paper in 1983, with no earlier implementation

questions.explanation: 40 years of near-continuity is the chapter's point. Almost all relational databases today, and some nonrelational databases, support transactions.

questions.question: What were NoSQL databases aiming for in the late 2000s, and what does the chapter call the main casualty?

options.text: New data models, replication and partitioning by default. Transactions were the main casualty of this movement: many of the new generation of databases abandoned transactions entirely, or redefined the word to describe a much weaker set of guarantees than had previously been understood
Stronger consistency; durability was the casualty
Better query languages; indexing was the casualty
Lower cost; replication was the casualty

questions.explanation: Redefining the word is the part that makes vendor claims hard to compare.

questions.question: What two opposing beliefs about transactions does the chapter dismiss, and how?

options.text: The belief that transactions are the antithesis of scalability and that any large-scale system must abandon them to maintain good performance and high availability, versus the vendor position that transactional guarantees are an essential requirement for 'serious applications' with 'valuable data'. Both viewpoints are pure hyperbole
It endorses the first and rejects the second
It endorses the second and rejects the first
It takes no position on either

questions.explanation: The truth is not that simple: like every other technical design choice, transactions have advantages and limitations, which the chapter explores both in normal operation and in various extreme but realistic circumstances.

questions.question: Expand ACID, and give its authors, year and motivation.

options.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability — coined in 1983 by Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter in an effort to establish precise terminology for fault-tolerance mechanisms in databases
Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Durability — coined by Jim Gray in 1981 for transaction processing
Availability, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — coined by Codd in 1970
Atomicity, Consistency, Integrity, Durability — coined by the SQL standard committee in 1992

questions.explanation: The irony the chapter notes: the term intended to establish precision has become imprecise.

questions.question: Why has ACID 'become mostly a marketing term'?

options.text: Because in practice one database's implementation of ACID does not equal another's: there is a lot of ambiguity around the meaning of isolation, so when a system claims to be ACID compliant it's unclear what guarantees you can actually expect
Because the acronym was trademarked
Because the properties are impossible to implement
Because most databases are not ACID compliant

questions.explanation: The high-level idea is sound, but the devil is in the details.

questions.question: Expand BASE, and give the chapter's assessment.

options.text: Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventual consistency — which is even more vague than the definition of ACID; it seems the only sensible definition of BASE is 'not ACID', so it can mean almost anything you want
Basic Atomicity, Serializability, Eventual durability — a precise weaker standard
Balanced Availability and Strong Eventual consistency — stricter than ACID
Best Available State Estimate — a consistency model

questions.explanation: Systems that do not meet the ACID criteria are sometimes called BASE, which is defined only negatively.

questions.question: Contrast the multi-threaded-programming meaning of 'atomic' with the ACID meaning.

options.text: In multi-threaded programming, if one thread executes an atomic operation there is no way another thread could see the half-finished result of that operation — the system can only be in the state it was before the operation or after the operation, not something in between. ACID atomicity is not about concurrency at all: it does not describe what happens if several processes try to access the same data at the same time, since that is covered under the letter I for isolation
They mean exactly the same thing
ACID atomicity is about concurrency; the threading sense is about durability
The threading sense is about crashes; the ACID sense is about locking

questions.explanation: A trap because the word is genuinely overloaded across branches of computing.

questions.question: What does ACID atomicity actually describe, and which example faults does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What happens if a client wants to make several writes but a fault occurs after some of the writes have been processed — the transaction is aborted and the database must discard or undo any writes it has made so far in that transaction
The process crashes, or the network connection is interrupted
The disk becomes full, or some integrity constraint is violated
Two clients write to the same object simultaneously

questions.explanation: The last one is isolation's territory, not atomicity's.

questions.question: Why is the absence of atomicity specifically a retry problem?

options.text: Because without atomicity, if an error occurs partway through you don't know how much of the multiple changes have already taken effect — so it's difficult to know which changes have taken effect and which haven't, and the application risks making the same change twice, leading to duplicate or incorrect data. Atomicity solves it by making the failed case knowable: the transaction didn't change anything, so it can safely be retried
Because retries always fail without atomicity
Because atomicity prevents retries entirely
Because retries require durability, not atomicity

questions.explanation: Knowability is what makes retry safe.

questions.question: Which word does the chapter say would have been better than 'atomicity', and why does it keep 'atomicity' anyway?

options.text: Abortability, since the ability to abort a transaction on error and have all writes from that transaction discarded is the defining feature of ACID atomicity — but the chapter sticks with atomicity since that's the usual word
Indivisibility, but the term is too long
Durability, but it is already taken
Isolation, but it would confuse readers

questions.explanation: Abortability names the mechanism; atomicity names the appearance.

questions.question: Match each usage of 'consistency' to its meaning. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In Chapter 5, replica consistency and eventual consistency in asynchronously replicated systems
In partitioning and rebalancing, consistent hashing
In the CAP theorem, linearizability
In ACID, an application-specific notion of the database being in a 'good state'

questions.explanation: It's unfortunate that the same word is used with at least four different meanings.

questions.question: Give the accounting example for ACID consistency, and say whose responsibility it is.

options.text: Consistency here means invariants about your data that must always be true — for example in an accounting system, credits and debits across all accounts must always be balanced. It is the application's responsibility to define its transactions correctly so they preserve invariants; that is not something the database can guarantee, although it can check some kinds such as foreign key constraints and uniqueness constraints
It means all replicas hold the same data, and is the database's responsibility
It means reads return the latest write, and is the client's responsibility
It means the schema is enforced, and is the administrator's responsibility

questions.explanation: Application-defined invariants are the ones the database cannot know about.

questions.question: What is the chapter's argument for evicting C from ACID?

options.text: Atomicity, isolation and durability are properties of the database, whereas consistency in the ACID sense is a property of the application — the application may rely on the database's atomicity and isolation properties in order to achieve consistency, but it's not up to the database alone. Thus the letter C doesn't really belong in ACID. A footnote adds that Joe Hellerstein remarked the C was tossed in to make the acronym work, and that it wasn't considered important at the time
That consistency is redundant with durability
That consistency is impossible to define
That consistency is the only property that matters

questions.explanation: A clean separation: three database properties and one application property.

questions.question: Two clients concurrently increment a counter, each doing read, add 1, write, starting from 42. What happens?

options.text: The counter should have increased from 42 to 44 since two increments happened, but it actually only went to 43 because of the race condition — assuming there is no increment operation built into the database. This is called a lost update
The counter reaches 44 correctly because writes are atomic
The counter reaches 42 because both writes are rejected
One client receives an error and the counter reaches 43

questions.explanation: Read-modify-write without isolation loses one of the two increments.

questions.question: How do the classic database textbooks formalize isolation, and what exactly does the database promise?

options.text: As serializability, meaning each transaction can pretend that it is the only transaction running on the entire database: the database ensures that when the transactions have committed, the result is the same as if they had run serially, one after another, even though in reality they may have run concurrently
As linearizability, meaning every read sees the latest write
As snapshot isolation, meaning reads come from a consistent snapshot
As atomicity, meaning transactions are indivisible

questions.explanation: Concurrently running transactions shouldn't be able to step on each other's toes.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about serializable isolation in practice, and about Oracle's 'serializable'?

options.text: In practice serializable isolation is rarely used because it carries a performance penalty; some popular databases such as Oracle 11g don't even implement it. Oracle has an isolation level called 'serializable', but it actually implements something weaker known as snapshot isolation
Serializable isolation is the default in most databases, and Oracle's implementation is genuine
Oracle's serializable level is stronger than the standard requires
Serializable isolation is free in modern databases

questions.explanation: The first of the chapter's several vocabulary traps around isolation-level names.

questions.question: Define durability, and what it means in single-node versus replicated databases.

options.text: The promise that once a transaction has committed successfully, any data it has written will not be forgotten, even if there is a hardware fault or the database crashes. In a single-node database it typically means the data has been written to nonvolatile storage, usually also involving a write-ahead log so data can be recovered if the data structures on disk are corrupted. In a replicated database it means the data has been successfully copied to some number of nodes — so the database must wait until these writes or replications are complete before reporting a transaction as successfully committed
That data survives in memory; replication is irrelevant
That data is written to a cache before commit
That data can be recovered from a nightly backup

questions.explanation: The chapter is clear that perfect durability does not exist: if all your hard disks and all your backups are destroyed at the same time, there's obviously nothing your database can do to save you.

questions.question: The 'Replication and Durability' sidebar traces what durability has meant. What are the stages?

options.text: Historically it meant writing to an archive tape; then it was understood as writing to a disk or SSD; more recently it has been adapted to mean replication. Asked which implementation is better, the sidebar answers that the truth is, nothing is perfect
It has always meant writing to disk, with no historical change
It meant replication first, then disk, then tape
It meant in-memory persistence, then disk

questions.explanation: Three stages, each superseding rather than abolishing the last.

questions.question: Which arguments does the sidebar give on disk versus replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For replication: if data is written to disk and the machine dies, the data isn't lost but it is inaccessible until the machine is repaired or transferred — replicated systems can remain available
For disk: a correlated fault such as a power outage or a bug that crashes on a particular input can knock out all replicas at once, so writing to disk is still relevant even for in-memory databases
For disk: in an asynchronously replicated system, recent writes may be lost when the leader becomes unavailable
Replication makes disk writes entirely unnecessary

questions.explanation: The two pull in opposite directions, which is why neither is sufficient alone.

questions.question: Which storage-reliability findings does the sidebar cite? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A study of SSDs found that between 30% and 80% of drives develop at least one bad block during the first four years of operation
Magnetic hard drives have a lower rate of bad sectors but a higher rate of complete failure than SSDs
On SSDs in particular, even fsync isn't guaranteed to work correctly; and an SSD disconnected from power can start losing data within a few weeks, depending on temperature
SSDs never develop bad blocks in the first four years

questions.explanation: Disk firmware can have bugs like any other software, subtle interactions between the storage engine and the filesystem can corrupt files after a crash, and if data has been corrupted for some time without being detected you need a historical backup. The conclusion: there is no one technique that can provide absolute guarantees — only risk-reduction techniques, which can and should be used together, and any theoretical guarantee should be taken with a healthy grain of salt.

questions.question: In the email counter example, why is the count stored in a separate field, and what does that oblige you to do?

options.text: Because a query counting unread messages may be too slow if there are many emails, so the number of unread messages is stored in a separate field — a kind of denormalization. That obliges you to increment the unread counter whenever a new message comes in, and decrement it whenever a message is marked as read
Because the schema requires it; no extra work is needed
Because counters cannot be computed in SQL
Because the field is indexed automatically

questions.explanation: Denormalization is what creates the multi-object write that needs a transaction.

questions.question: What does user 2 see in Figure 7-2, and what is the anomaly called?

options.text: The mailbox listing shows an unread message, but the counter shows zero unread messages because the counter increment has not yet happened. This is a dirty read: one transaction reads another transaction's uncommitted writes. Isolation prevents it by ensuring user 2 sees either both the inserted email and the updated counter, or neither, but not an inconsistent halfway point
User 2 sees the counter but not the message; it is a lost update
User 2 sees neither; it is write skew
User 2 sees both; there is no anomaly

questions.explanation: A footnote defends the example by noting that arguably the counter is an optimization that could be dropped, but a customer account balance in a payment transaction cannot be.

questions.question: Figure 7-2 illustrated isolation. What does Figure 7-3 illustrate?

options.text: Atomicity: without it, if an error occurs partway through the multiple writes, the mailbox and the counter go out of sync — with atomicity, if the counter update fails the inserted email is rolled back and undone, so the two stay consistent
Durability, using the same example
Consistency, using a different example
Serializability, using the counter race

questions.explanation: Same example, different ACID property — isolation is about other readers, atomicity about partial failure.

questions.question: How do relational databases decide which operations belong to the same transaction, and what problem does a footnote raise?

options.text: On the basis of the client's TCP connection to the database server: on any particular connection, everything between a BEGIN TRANSACTION statement and a COMMIT statement is considered part of the same transaction. The footnote calls this not ideal: if the TCP connection is interrupted after the client has requested a commit but before the server acknowledges, the client doesn't know whether the transaction was committed or not — the problem can be solved by a transaction manager that groups operations by a unique transaction identifier that is not bound to a particular TCP connection
By session cookie; the footnote notes cookies can be forged
By a per-statement identifier; the footnote notes it is expensive
By a lock table; the footnote notes locks can be lost

questions.explanation: The footnote cites 'The End-to-End Argument for Databases'.

questions.question: Many nonrelational databases offer a multi-put API. Why doesn't that resolve the lack of transactions?

options.text: Because such a batch-like operation does not necessarily have transaction semantics: the command may succeed for some keys and fail for others, for example if part of the operation times out — leaving the database in a partially updated state
Because multi-put is slower than individual writes
Because multi-put cannot touch more than one key
It does resolve it; multi-put is a transaction

questions.explanation: A batch API is not an atomicity guarantee.

questions.question: You are writing a 20 KB JSON document. What questions does the chapter ask about single-object writes, and what do storage engines aim to provide?

options.text: If the network connection is interrupted after the first 10 KB have been sent, does the database store that unparseable 10 KB fragment? If the power fails while the database is overwriting the previous value on disk, do you end up with the old and new values spliced together? If another client reads the document while the write is in progress, will it see a partially updated value? Because these would be incredibly confusing, storage engines almost universally aim to provide atomicity and isolation on the level of a single object — such as a key-value pair — on one node, typically implemented using a log for crash recovery and a lock on each object
Whether the document is indexed, compressed and replicated; engines aim for durability only
Whether the schema is validated; engines aim for consistency only
Whether the write is fast; engines aim for throughput only

questions.explanation: Single-object atomicity and isolation are essentially universal, unlike multi-object transactions.

questions.question: Which more complex single-object operations does the chapter name, and what do they save you from?

options.text: An increment operation, which removes the need for a read-modify-write cycle like the one in the counter race; and a compare-and-set operation, which allows a write to happen only if the value has not been concurrently changed by someone else. A footnote notes that strictly speaking the term atomic increment uses the word atomic in the sense of multi-threaded programming — in the ACID sense it would be isolated or serializable
Bulk insert and bulk delete, which save you from locking
Snapshot read and range scan, which save you from phantoms
Commit and rollback, which save you from crashes

questions.explanation: Both remove a read-modify-write cycle from the application.

questions.question: Some vendors call single-object operations 'lightweight transactions'. Why does the chapter refuse the term?

options.text: Because although such operations are useful and can prevent lost updates, they are not transactions in the usual sense: the word is generally understood as a mechanism for grouping multiple operations on multiple objects into one unit of execution, so calling them transactions — sometimes even 'ACID' — is misleading marketing
Because they are too slow to be called transactions
Because they lack durability
Because they only work on a single node

questions.explanation: Multiple objects is the defining criterion the term requires.

questions.question: Which cases genuinely need multi-object transactions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Relational or graph data with references: when a row has a foreign key reference to a row in another table, or when inserting several vertices and edges, you need to ensure these references remain valid or the data becomes nonsensical
Denormalized documents: document databases lack join functionality and so encourage denormalization, so when updating denormalized information you need to update several documents in one go
Databases with secondary indexes: these indexes are different database objects from a transaction point of view, so without isolation it's possible for a record to appear in one index but not another
Single-key counters, which cannot be incremented safely otherwise

questions.explanation: Single-key counters are exactly what atomic single-object operations handle. The chapter concedes such applications can still be implemented without transactions, but error handling becomes much more complicated without atomicity and the lack of isolation can cause concurrency problems.

questions.question: Why have many distributed datastores abandoned multi-object transactions, and does the chapter accept this as fundamental?

options.text: Because they are difficult to implement across partitions, and they can get in the way in some scenarios where very high availability or performance is required. But there is nothing that fundamentally prevents transactions in a distributed database, and Chapter 9 discusses implementations of distributed transactions
Because transactions are mathematically impossible in a distributed system
Because the CAP theorem forbids them
Because no one has attempted to implement them

questions.explanation: Difficult and sometimes unwanted, not impossible.

questions.question: What philosophy do ACID databases follow on aborts, and who rejects it?

options.text: They follow the philosophy that they would rather abandon the transaction entirely than allow it to remain half-finished. Datastores with leaderless replication work much more on a best-effort basis: the database will do as much as it can, and if it runs into an error it won't undo something it has already done — so it's the application's responsibility to recover from errors
ACID databases retry automatically; leaderless systems abort
Both families abort identically
ACID databases never abort

questions.explanation: Abortability is the ACID stance; best effort is the leaderless one.

questions.question: Which ORM frameworks does the chapter name, and what do they fail to do?

options.text: Rails's ActiveRecord and Django; they don't retry aborted transactions — instead the error usually results in an exception bubbling up the stack, so any user input is thrown away and they get an error message. That's a shame, because the whole point of aborts is to enable safe retries
Hibernate and Entity Framework; they retry too aggressively
SQLAlchemy and Sequelize; they suppress all errors
They all retry correctly; the chapter praises them

questions.explanation: An abortable transaction that isn't retried wastes the guarantee.

questions.question: Retrying an aborted transaction 'isn't perfect'. Which caveats does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the transaction actually succeeded but the network failed while the server tried to acknowledge the commit, retrying causes it to be performed twice — unless you have an additional application-level deduplication mechanism in place
If the error is due to overload, retrying will make the problem worse, not better; you can limit the number of retries, use exponential backoff, and handle overload-related errors differently

It is only worth retrying after transient errors such as deadlock, isolation violation, temporary network interruptions and failover — after a permanent error such as a constraint violation a retry would be pointless

If the transaction has side effects outside the database, such as sending an email, those may happen even if the transaction is aborted; two-phase commit can help. And if the client process fails while retrying, any data it was trying to write is lost

questions.explanation: Five caveats. Retrying is simple and effective but not unconditional.

questions.question: Under what conditions do race conditions come into play?

options.text: Only if one transaction reads data that is concurrently modified by another transaction, or if two transactions try to simultaneously modify the same data — if two transactions don't touch the same data they can safely be run in parallel
Whenever two transactions run at the same time, regardless of data
Only when transactions span multiple partitions
Only under serializable isolation

questions.explanation: Data overlap, not mere simultaneity, is the precondition.

questions.question: Why do concurrency bugs resist testing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They are hard to find by testing, because such bugs are only triggered when you get unlucky with the timing — which may happen very rarely and is usually difficult to reproduce
Concurrency is difficult to reason about, especially in a large application where you don't necessarily know which other pieces of code are accessing the database
Application development is difficult enough with just one user at a time, but having many concurrent users makes it much harder, because any piece of data could unexpectedly change at any time
Test frameworks cannot run more than one transaction

questions.explanation: Rarity, irreproducibility and non-local reasoning all work against testing.

questions.question: What is transaction isolation for, and what is the practical problem?

options.text: Databases have long tried to hide concurrency issues from application developers by providing transaction isolation: in theory, serializable isolation makes the database guarantee that transactions have the same effect as if they ran serially, so the developer can pretend that no concurrency is happening. In practice, isolation is unfortunately not that simple — serializable isolation has a performance cost, so systems commonly use weaker levels of isolation which protect against some concurrency issues but not all
Isolation is free and always enabled at the strongest level
Isolation exists only for auditing purposes
Isolation guarantees nothing in any real database

questions.explanation: Some, not all — which is why the chapter enumerates the specific anomalies each level permits.

questions.question: What real-world harm does the chapter attribute to weak isolation bugs, and why does 'use an ACID database for financial data' miss the point? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They have caused substantial loss of money
They have led to investigation by financial auditors
They have caused customer data to be corrupted
The advice misses the point because even many popular relational database systems, usually considered 'ACID', use weak isolation — so they wouldn't necessarily have prevented these bugs

questions.explanation: The ACID label buys you nothing if the configured isolation level is weak. Rather than blindly relying on tools, we need to develop a good understanding of the kinds of concurrency problems that exist and how to prevent them.

questions.question: State read committed's two guarantees.

options.text: When reading from the database, you will only see data that has been committed — no dirty reads. When writing to the database, you will only overwrite data that has been committed — no dirty writes
Reads come from a consistent snapshot, and writes never block
Transactions execute in a serial order, and aborts are always safe
Reads are repeatable, and phantoms are prevented

questions.explanation: Read committed is the most basic level of transaction isolation. A footnote notes some databases support an even weaker level called read uncommitted, which prevents dirty writes but does not prevent dirty reads.

questions.question: Define a dirty read and the visibility rule read committed enforces.

options.text: A dirty read occurs when a transaction has written some data to the database but has not yet committed or aborted, and another transaction can see that uncommitted data. With read committed, any writes by a transaction only become visible to others when that transaction commits — and then all of its writes become visible at once
A dirty read is reading data that was later deleted; read committed prevents it by locking
A dirty read is reading from a stale replica; read committed routes reads to the leader
A dirty read is reading an aborted write; read committed retries the read

questions.explanation: In Figure 7-4, x starts at 2, user 1 sets x = 3 but has not yet committed, user 2 reads the old value 2, and only after user 1 commits does user 2 see 3.

questions.question: Why is it useful to prevent dirty reads? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Partial updates are visible: if a transaction updates several objects, a dirty read means another transaction may see some of the updates but not others — which is confusing to users and may cause other transactions to take incorrect decisions

Rolled-back data may be observed: if a transaction aborts, any writes it made are rolled back, so without preventing dirty reads a transaction may see data that is later rolled back and was never actually committed — which is mind-bending
Dirty reads cause data corruption on disk
Dirty reads violate durability

questions.explanation: Two reasons: partial visibility and observing writes that never happened.

questions.question: Define a dirty write and how databases prevent it.

options.text: If two transactions concurrently try to update the same object in a database, we assume the later write overwrites the earlier write — but if the earlier write is part of a transaction that has not yet committed, so the later write overwrites an uncommitted value, that is a dirty write. Transactions running at read committed must prevent dirty writes, usually by delaying the second write until the first write's transaction has committed or aborted
A dirty write is writing to an uncommitted read; prevented by snapshots
A dirty write is writing to a stale replica; prevented by quorums
A dirty write is an aborted write; prevented by logging

questions.explanation: Overwriting an uncommitted value is the definition.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-5, where Alice and Bob simultaneously try to buy the same car.

options.text: Buying a car requires two writes: the listing on the website needs to be updated to reflect the buyer, and the sales invoice needs to be sent to the buyer. With dirty writes, conflicting writes from different transactions can be mixed up — the sale is awarded to Bob but the invoice is sent to Alice. Read committed prevents such mishaps
Both buyers receive invoices and the sale is awarded to neither
The second transaction is rejected, so no mishap occurs even without read committed
Alice gets both the sale and the invoice; the anomaly is a lost update

questions.explanation: Two writes from two transactions interleaving is exactly what dirty-write prevention stops.

questions.question: Read committed prevents dirty writes. Why doesn't that fix the counter race?

options.text: Because the second increment's write happens after the first transaction has committed, so it isn't a dirty write — the increment is still lost, but for a different reason: it is a lost update, addressed separately
Because the counter is a single object, so isolation does not apply
Because read committed does not prevent dirty writes after all
It does fix it; the counter race cannot occur under read committed

questions.explanation: The two writes are sequential with respect to commit, so no uncommitted value is overwritten.

questions.question: Which databases does the chapter list as defaulting to read committed?

options.text: Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012 and MemSQL, among many others — making it a very popular isolation level
MySQL, MongoDB and Cassandra
DB2 and Riak
No mainstream database defaults to read committed

questions.explanation: Very widely deployed, which is why its anomalies matter in practice.

questions.question: Describe the row-level locking protocol that prevents dirty writes.

options.text: When a transaction wants to modify a particular object — a row or a document — it must first acquire a lock on that object, and hold that lock until the transaction is committed or aborted. Only one transaction can hold the lock for any given object; if another transaction wants to write to the same object it must wait until the first is committed or aborted. This locking is done automatically by databases in read committed mode or stronger
Locks are held only for the duration of the write statement
Locks are taken by the application explicitly
No locks are used; timestamps order the writes

questions.explanation: Held to end of transaction, acquired automatically.

questions.question: One option for preventing dirty reads is a brief read lock. Why does the chapter reject it?

options.text: Because it would mean one long-running write transaction can force many read-only transactions to wait until the long-running transaction has completed, which harms the response time of read-only transactions and is bad for operability: a slowdown in one part of an application can have a knock-on effect in a completely different part, due to waiting for locks
Because read locks cannot be implemented efficiently
Because read locks cause deadlock
Because read locks violate durability

questions.explanation: Operational coupling across unrelated parts of the application is the objection.

questions.question: How do most databases actually prevent dirty reads?

options.text: For every object that is written, the database remembers both the old committed value and the new value set by the transaction that currently holds the write lock; while the transaction is ongoing, any other transactions that read the object are simply given the old value. Only when the new value is committed do transactions switch over to reading the new value
By taking a read lock on every read
By aborting all concurrent readers
By delaying all reads until no writes are in flight

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that at the time of writing, the only databases that use locks for read committed isolation are IBM DB2 and Microsoft SQL Server in the read_committed_snapshot=off configuration.

questions.question: Alice has $1,000 split across two accounts of $500 each, and a transaction transfers $100 between them. What can Alice observe under read committed?

options.text: If she looks at her list of balances in the same moment as the transaction is being processed, she may see one account balance before the incoming payment has arrived — still $500 — and the other after the outgoing transfer has been made, $400 — so her total appears to be $900 and it seems $100 has vanished into thin air. Reloading would show $600 and $400 for a correct total
She always sees a correct total of $1,000
She sees $1,100, as if money were created
She sees an error rather than a balance

questions.explanation: Alice observes the database in an inconsistent state, even though each value she read was committed at the time she read it.

questions.question: Name the anomaly and say whether read committed is violated.

options.text: It is called a nonrepeatable read or read skew, and read committed is not violated by it: read skew is considered acceptable under read committed isolation, because the account balances Alice saw were indeed committed at the time when she read them
It is a dirty read, and read committed is violated
It is a lost update, and read committed is violated
It is write skew, and read committed is violated

questions.explanation: A boxed warning notes the term skew is overloaded: it was previously used for an unbalanced workload with hot spots, whereas here it means a timing anomaly — nothing to do with hot spots.

questions.question: Alice's read skew resolves on reload. Which workloads cannot tolerate it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Backups: taking a backup requires making a copy of the entire database, which may take hours on a large database, and during that time writes will continue to be made — so you may end up with some parts of the backup containing an older version of the data and other parts containing a newer version. If you then restore from that backup, the inconsistencies such as disappearing money become permanent

Analytic queries and integrity checks: queries that scan over large parts of the database — perhaps for analytics, or a periodic integrity check monitoring for data corruption — are likely to return nonsensical results if they observe parts of the database at different points in time
Single-key point lookups
Atomic increments

questions.explanation: Both read large amounts of data over a long window, which is exactly what read skew corrupts.

questions.question: Define snapshot isolation.

options.text: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database: the transaction sees all the data that was committed in the database at the start of the transaction, and even if the data is subsequently changed by another transaction, each transaction sees only the old data from that particular point in time
Each transaction reads the latest committed value at the time of each statement
Each transaction holds read locks for its duration
Each transaction executes serially on one thread

questions.explanation: It is a boon for long-running, read-only queries such as backups and analytics, because the data does not change under the query. It is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL with the InnoDB storage engine, Oracle and SQL Server, among others.

questions.question: What locking does snapshot isolation use, and what is the resulting mantra?

options.text: Implementations typically use write locks to prevent dirty writes, so a transaction that makes a write can block the progress of another transaction that writes to the same object — but reads do not require any locks. The key principle: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers, which allows the database to handle long-running read queries on a consistent snapshot at the same time as processing writes normally, without any lock contention between the two
It uses read locks and write locks; readers block writers and vice versa
It uses no locks at all; conflicts are detected at commit
It uses table-level locks only

questions.explanation: This mantra is precisely what two-phase locking inverts.

questions.question: Why must the database keep several versions of an object, and what is the technique called?

options.text: Because the database must potentially keep several different committed versions of an object, as various in-progress transactions may need to see the state of the database at different points in time. Since it maintains several versions of an object side by side, the technique is known as multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)
Because writes are append-only; the technique is log-structured storage
Because replicas diverge; the technique is version vectors
Because indexes need old values; the technique is copy-on-write

questions.explanation: Multiple in-flight snapshot points is what forces multiple versions.

questions.question: How do read committed and snapshot isolation differ in an MVCC engine?

options.text: If a database only needed to provide read committed isolation it would be sufficient to keep two versions of an object — the committed version and the overwritten-but-not-yet-committed version. But storage engines that support snapshot isolation typically use MVCC for their read committed isolation level as well; the typical approach is that read committed uses a separate snapshot for each query, while snapshot isolation uses the same snapshot for an entire transaction
Read committed needs four versions; snapshot isolation needs two
Read committed uses one snapshot per transaction; snapshot isolation uses one per query
They are implemented identically

questions.explanation: Per-query versus per-transaction snapshot is the whole distinction.

questions.question: How are transaction IDs assigned in the PostgreSQL implementation?

options.text: Each transaction is given a unique, always-increasing transaction ID (txid); whenever a transaction writes anything to the database, the data it writes is tagged with the transaction ID of the writer. A footnote notes that transaction IDs are 32-bit integers, so they overflow after approximately 4 billion transactions — PostgreSQL's vacuum process performs cleanup which ensures that overflow does not affect the data
Transaction IDs are random UUIDs, so no overflow is possible
Transaction IDs are wall-clock timestamps
Transaction IDs are reused after each commit

questions.explanation: Always-increasing is the property the visibility rules depend on.

questions.question: Describe the two per-row fields in the MVCC table, and what happens on a delete.

options.text: Each row has a created_by field containing the ID of the transaction that inserted this row into the table, and a deleted_by field which is initially empty. When a transaction deletes a row, the row isn't actually deleted from the database but marked for deletion by setting deleted_by to the requesting transaction's ID. Later, when it is certain that no transaction can any longer access the deleted data, a garbage collection process removes any rows marked for deletion and frees their space
Each row has a version number and a checksum; deletes remove the row immediately
Each row has a lock field and a timestamp; deletes set the timestamp to zero
Each row has only a created_by field; deletes append a tombstone row

questions.explanation: Marking rather than removing is what lets older snapshots still see the row.

questions.question: How is an update represented internally, and what does the accounts table contain after transaction 13 deducts $100 from account 2?

options.text: An update is internally translated into a delete and a create — so the table actually contains two rows for account 2: the one with balance $500 was marked as deleted by transaction 13, and the one with balance $400 was created by transaction 13
The single row's balance field is overwritten in place from $500 to $400
A new table is created holding the new value
The old row is deleted immediately and only the new row remains

questions.explanation: Delete-plus-create is what makes an update a new version rather than a mutation.

questions.question: Which visibility rules let a transaction observe a consistent snapshot? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the start of each transaction, the database makes a list of all the other transactions that are in progress at that time; any writes those transactions have made are ignored, even if the transactions subsequently commit
Any writes made by aborted transactions are ignored
Any writes made by transactions with a later transaction ID are ignored, regardless of whether those transactions have committed
All other writes are visible to the application's queries — and these rules apply to both creation and deletion of objects

questions.explanation: Four rules, applying symmetrically to creates and deletes.

questions.question: Why does transaction 12 see $500 for account 2 in Figure 7-7, and what is the two-condition restatement of the rules?

options.text: The deletion of the $500 row was made by transaction 13, and by rule 3 transaction 12 cannot see a deletion made by transaction 13; the creation of the $400 row is likewise not yet visible. So transaction 12 sees the balance as $500. Restated: an object is visible if, at the time when the reader's transaction started, the transaction that created the object had already committed; and the object is not marked for deletion, or if it is, the transaction that requested deletion had not yet committed at the time when the reader's transaction started
Because transaction 12 holds a read lock on the row
Because transaction 13 aborted
Because transaction 12 started after transaction 13 committed

questions.explanation: A long-running transaction may continue using a snapshot for a long time, continuing to read values that other transactions have since overwritten or deleted. By never updating values in place but instead creating a new version every time a value is changed, the database can provide a consistent snapshot at only a small overhead.

questions.question: How can indexes work in a multi-version database?

options.text: One option is to have the index simply point to all versions of an object and require an index query to filter out any object versions that are not visible to the current transaction; when garbage collection removes old object versions that are no longer visible to any transaction, the corresponding index entries can also be removed. In practice many implementation details determine the performance — PostgreSQL, for example, has optimizations for avoiding index updates if different versions of the same object can fit on the same page
Indexes must be rebuilt on every write
Indexes point only to the newest version, so old versions are unindexed
Multi-version databases cannot have indexes

questions.explanation: Point at all versions and filter on read, garbage-collecting index entries alongside rows.

questions.question: Describe the append-only / copy-on-write B-tree approach and which systems use it.

options.text: CouchDB, Datomic and LMDB use append-only/copy-on-write B-trees which do not overwrite pages of the tree when they are updated, but instead create a new copy of each modified page; parent pages, up to the root of the tree, are copied and updated to point to the new versions of their child pages. Any pages that are not affected by a write do not need to be copied and remain immutable. With append-only B-trees, every write transaction (or batch of transactions) creates a new B-tree root, and a root created at a particular point in time is a consistent snapshot of the database at that time — so there is no need to filter out objects based on transaction IDs, since subsequent writes cannot modify an existing B-tree, only create new tree roots. However, this approach also requires a background process for compaction and garbage collection
PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle use it; it requires no garbage collection
It overwrites pages in place but keeps a version stamp per page
It copies the entire tree on every write

questions.explanation: Immutability gives snapshots for free, at the cost of compaction.

questions.question: What does each vendor call snapshot isolation, and why do the names diverge?

options.text: Oracle calls it serializable, and PostgreSQL and MySQL call it repeatable read; IBM DB2 uses 'repeatable read' to refer to serializability. The names diverge because the SQL standard doesn't have the concept of snapshot isolation — its definition of isolation levels is based on System R's 1975 definition, and snapshot isolation hadn't yet been invented then. Instead, databases look at what is superficially similar in the standard: repeatable read, whose requirements snapshot isolation meets, so implementers can claim standards compliance
All vendors call it snapshot isolation; the standard defines it explicitly
Oracle calls it repeatable read and PostgreSQL calls it serializable
The SQL standard defines snapshot isolation, and vendors deviate arbitrarily

questions.explanation: A gap in a 1975-derived standard is what produced the naming chaos.

questions.question: Give the chapter's indictment of the SQL standard's isolation levels.

options.text: The standard's definition of isolation levels is flawed: it is ambiguous, imprecise, and not as implementation-independent as a standard should be. Even though several databases implement repeatable read there are big differences in the guarantees they actually provide, despite being ostensibly standardized. There has been a formal definition of repeatable read in the research literature, but most implementations don't satisfy that formal definition — as a result, nobody really knows what repeatable read means
The standard is precise and implementations are consistent
The standard has no definition of isolation levels at all
The standard is precise but too strict for implementers

questions.explanation: 'Nobody really knows what repeatable read means' is the closing verdict.

questions.question: Define the lost update problem and the verb the chapter uses.

options.text: It occurs if an application reads some value from the database, modifies it, and writes back the modified value — a read-modify-write cycle. If two transactions do this concurrently, one of the modifications can be lost because the second write does not include the first modification: we sometimes say that the later write clobbers the earlier write. It is the best known of the write-write conflict problems
It occurs when a write is rolled back on commit; the verb is discard
It occurs when a replica misses a write; the verb is drop
It occurs when two transactions read the same value; the verb is stale

questions.explanation: Read committed and snapshot isolation were primarily about what a read-only transaction can see in the presence of concurrent writes; this section turns to two transactions writing concurrently.

questions.question: Which read-modify-write scenarios does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Incrementing a counter or updating an account balance — requires reading the current value, calculating the new value, and writing back the updated value
Making a local change to a complex value, for example adding an element to a list within a JSON document — requires parsing the document, making the change, and writing back the modified document
Two users editing a wiki page at the same time, where each user saves their changes by sending the entire page contents to the server, overwriting whatever is currently in the database
Reading a row by primary key with no subsequent write

questions.explanation: Three scenarios, all sharing the read-modify-write shape.

questions.question: Which solution does the chapter call the best, and which systems does it name?

options.text: Atomic write operations, which remove the need to implement read-modify-write cycles in application code: an SQL update that increments a column by referring to its own current value is concurrency-safe in most relational databases, MongoDB provides atomic operations for making local modifications to a part of a JSON document, and Redis provides atomic operations for modifying data structures such as priority queues. They are usually the best solution if your code can be expressed in terms of those operations
Explicit locking, which is always safest
Last write wins, which is simplest
Compare-and-set, which is universally supported

questions.explanation: Not all writes can easily be expressed as atomic operations — for example updates to a wiki page involve arbitrary text editing. A footnote notes it is possible, albeit fairly complicated, to express the editing of a text document as a stream of atomic mutations.

questions.question: How are atomic operations implemented?

options.text: Usually by taking an exclusive lock on the object when it is read so that no other transaction can read it until the update has been applied — a technique sometimes known as cursor stability. Another option is to simply force all atomic operations to be executed on a single thread
By optimistic retry with no locking
By snapshot isolation alone
By two-phase commit

questions.explanation: Cursor stability is the name for the read-with-exclusive-lock approach.

questions.question: What does the chapter say ORM frameworks do to lost-update safety?

options.text: They make it easy to accidentally write code that performs unsafe read-modify-write cycles instead of using atomic operations provided by the database — which isn't a problem if you know what you're doing, but is potentially a source of subtle bugs that are difficult to find by testing
They automatically convert read-modify-write into atomic operations
They prevent all lost updates by default
They have no bearing on lost updates

questions.explanation: The convenience of the abstraction hides the unsafe pattern.

questions.question: In the multiplayer game example, why is an atomic operation insufficient and what does the SQL do?

options.text: Because the application also needs to ensure that a player's move abides by the rules of the game, which involves some logic that you cannot sensibly implement as a database query. So the transaction selects the position with a FOR UPDATE clause, which indicates that the database should take a lock on all rows returned by this query — preventing two players from concurrently moving the same piece
Because atomic operations cannot touch more than one row; FOR UPDATE creates a snapshot
Because the game is distributed; FOR UPDATE replicates the lock
An atomic operation is sufficient; FOR UPDATE is redundant

questions.explanation: Application logic that can't be pushed into the database is what forces explicit locking. The catch: to get it right you need to carefully think about your application logic, and it's easy to forget to add a necessary lock somewhere.

questions.question: Contrast automatic lost update detection with locks and atomic operations.

options.text: Locks and atomic write operations prevent lost updates by forcing the read-modify-write cycles to happen sequentially. An alternative is to allow them to execute in parallel and, if the transaction manager detects a lost update, abort the transaction and force it to retry its read-modify-write cycle. An advantage is that databases can perform this check efficiently in conjunction with snapshot isolation
Detection is slower than locking in all cases
Detection requires serial execution
Detection and locking are the same mechanism

questions.explanation: Optimistic parallel execution plus abort-on-detect, riding on MVCC bookkeeping.

questions.question: Which isolation levels automatically detect lost updates? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL's repeatable read
Oracle's serializable
SQL Server's snapshot isolation level
MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read

questions.explanation: MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read does not detect lost updates. Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates in order to qualify as providing snapshot isolation, so MySQL does not provide snapshot isolation under this definition.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call lost update detection 'a great feature'?

options.text: Because it doesn't require application code to use any special database features — you may forget to use a lock or an atomic operation and thus introduce a bug, but lost update detection happens automatically and is thus less error-prone
Because it is faster than locking
Because it works across replicas
Because it never aborts transactions

questions.explanation: Safety that does not depend on the developer remembering something.

questions.question: Describe compare-and-set for the wiki page, and when it isn't safe.

options.text: In databases without transactions you sometimes find an atomic compare-and-set operation, which avoids lost updates by allowing an update to happen only if the value has not changed since you last read it: the update includes the previously-read content in its WHERE clause. If the content has changed and no longer matches, this update will have no effect, so you need to check whether the update took effect and retry if necessary. But if the database allows the WHERE clause to read from an old snapshot, this statement may not prevent lost updates, because the condition may be true even though another concurrent write is occurring — so check whether your database's compare-and-set operation is safe before relying on it
Compare-and-set is always safe in every database
Compare-and-set requires an exclusive lock, making it equivalent to FOR UPDATE
Compare-and-set cannot be expressed in SQL

questions.explanation: A stale-snapshot WHERE clause silently defeats the mechanism.

questions.question: Why don't lock and compare-and-set techniques transfer to multi-leader or leaderless replication, and what is used instead?

options.text: Because locks and compare-and-set assume that there is a single up-to-date copy of the data. Databases with multi-leader or leaderless replication allow several writes to happen concurrently and replicate them asynchronously, so they cannot guarantee that there is a single up-to-date copy of the data — thus techniques based on locks or compare-and-set do not apply. Instead, a common approach is to allow concurrent writes to create several conflicting versions of a value, also known as siblings, and to use application code or special data structures to resolve and merge these versions after the fact
Because replication is synchronous; quorums are used instead
Because locks are too slow; timestamps are used instead
They do transfer without modification

questions.explanation: No single up-to-date copy means nothing to lock against.

questions.question: Which kind of operation works well in a replicated context, and what default does the chapter warn against?

options.text: Commutative atomic operations, which you can apply in a different order on different replicas and still get the same result — for example incrementing a counter or adding an element to a set. Riak 2.0 datatypes prevent lost updates across replicas: when a value is concurrently updated by different clients Riak automatically merges the updates in such a way that no updates are lost. The warning: last write wins (LWW) conflict resolution is prone to lost updates, and unfortunately LWW is the default in many replicated databases
Non-commutative operations work best; LWW is safe
Only read-only operations work; LWW is recommended
Commutative operations are unsafe; locks are recommended

questions.explanation: Order-independence is what makes merging possible without coordination.

questions.question: State the hospital on-call invariant and when a doctor may give up a shift.

options.text: The hospital usually tries to have several doctors on call at any one time, but it absolutely must have at least one doctor on call. Doctors can give up their shifts — for example if they are sick themselves — provided that at least one colleague remains on call in that shift
Exactly two doctors must be on call at all times, with no exceptions
Doctors may never give up shifts
At least three doctors must be on call, and any may leave

questions.explanation: 'At least one' is the invariant the write skew violates.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-8 where Alice and Bob both click 'go off call' simultaneously under snapshot isolation.

options.text: The application first checks that two or more doctors are currently on call; if yes, it assumes it's safe for one doctor to go off call. Since the database is using snapshot isolation, both checks return 2, so both transactions proceed. Alice updates her own record to take herself off call and Bob updates his own record likewise. Both transactions commit, and now no doctor is on call — the requirement of having at least one doctor on call has been violated
One check returns 2 and the other returns 1, so only Alice succeeds
Both checks return 1, so neither proceeds
Snapshot isolation prevents this; the second transaction aborts

questions.explanation: Figure 7-8's caption: example of write skew causing an application bug.

questions.question: Why is write skew neither a dirty write nor a lost update?

options.text: Because the two transactions are updating two different objects — Alice's and Bob's on-call records respectively. It is less obvious that a conflict occurred here, but it's definitely a race condition: if the two transactions had run one after another, the second doctor would have been prevented from going off call. The anomalous behaviour was only possible because the transactions ran concurrently
Because no writes occurred at all
Because both transactions updated the same object
Because the transactions were serialized

questions.explanation: Different objects written, shared premise read — that is the shape of write skew.

questions.question: State the general definition of write skew, and how the other anomalies fall out of it.

options.text: Write skew can occur if two transactions read the same objects and then update some of those objects — different transactions may update different objects, and in the general case you get write skew. In the special case where different transactions update the same object, you get a dirty write or lost update anomaly, depending on the timing. So write skew is a generalization of the lost update problem
Write skew is a special case of lost update
Write skew and lost update are unrelated
Write skew is a special case of dirty read

questions.explanation: The general case first, with the same-object cases as specializations.

questions.question: Which of these prevent write skew automatically: PostgreSQL's repeatable read, MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable, SQL Server's snapshot isolation?

options.text: None of them — write skew is not automatically detected. Automatically preventing write skew requires true serializable isolation, and atomic single-object operations don't help either, since multiple objects are involved
All four prevent it
Only Oracle's serializable prevents it
Only PostgreSQL's repeatable read prevents it

questions.explanation: Note the contrast with lost updates: three of those four do detect lost updates, but none detects write skew.

questions.question: Could a database constraint enforce the on-call rule?

options.text: Not easily: most constraints — uniqueness, foreign key constraints, or restrictions on a particular value — involve only a single object, whereas 'at least one doctor must be on call' would need a constraint that involves multiple objects. Most databases do not have built-in support for such constraints, though you may be able to implement them with triggers or materialized views
Yes, a uniqueness constraint suffices
Yes, a foreign key constraint suffices
No, and no workaround exists

questions.explanation: Multi-object constraints are the gap. If you can't use a serializable isolation level, the second-best option is probably to explicitly lock the rows the transaction depends on with SELECT FOR UPDATE.

questions.question: In the meeting room booking example, what is being enforced and why does it fail?

options.text: It enforces that there cannot be two bookings for the same meeting room at the same time: the transaction first checks for conflicting bookings — bookings for the same room with an overlapping time range — and if none are found, creates the meeting. But snapshot isolation does not prevent another user from concurrently inserting a conflicting meeting, so to guarantee you won't get scheduling conflicts you once again need serializable isolation
It enforces room capacity, and fails because of lost updates
It enforces booking duration, and fails because of dirty reads
It succeeds under snapshot isolation

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that PostgreSQL's range types make it possible to define a constraint here elegantly, but they are not widely supported in other databases.

questions.question: The multiplayer game appeared earlier under lost updates. What different problem does it illustrate here?

options.text: A lock on a row can prevent lost updates when two players try to move the same figure, but it doesn't prevent players from moving two different figures to the same position on the board, or otherwise violating the rules of the game. Depending on the kind of rule you are enforcing you might be able to use a unique constraint, but otherwise you're vulnerable to write skew
It illustrates dirty reads rather than write skew
It illustrates phantoms in read-only queries
It illustrates deadlock under 2PL

questions.explanation: Different objects, same shared rule — the write skew signature.

questions.question: Describe the username write skew and why this case is easier than the others.

options.text: On a website where each user has a unique username, two users may try to create accounts with the same username at the same time; you may use a transaction to check whether a name is taken and, if not, create an account with that name — but that is not safe under snapshot isolation. Fortunately a unique constraint is a simple solution here: the second transaction that tries to register the username will be aborted due to violating the constraint
It is harder because usernames are not indexable
It requires materializing conflicts
It requires serializable isolation with no simpler option

questions.explanation: The invariant happens to be exactly a single-object uniqueness rule, which databases do support.

questions.question: Describe the double-spending implementation and how write skew breaks it.

options.text: A service that lets users spend money or points needs to check that a user doesn't spend more than they have. You might implement this by inserting a tentative spending item into a user's account, listing all the items in the account, and checking that the sum is positive. With write skew it could happen that two spending items are inserted concurrently that together cause the balance to go negative, but neither transaction notices the other
The balance is overwritten by a lost update
A dirty read shows a stale balance
The implementation is safe under snapshot isolation

questions.explanation: Each transaction's sum is computed on a snapshot that excludes the other's insert.

questions.question: For which write-skew examples does the chapter say a database constraint is a workable fix? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Claiming a username — a unique constraint is a simple solution here
The multiplayer game — sometimes, depending on the kind of rule, a unique constraint may work
The doctor on call — no, it would need a constraint involving multiple objects
The meeting room booking — no, you once again need serializable isolation, though PostgreSQL range types can help

questions.explanation: All four statements are accurate: two are workable (one fully, one conditionally) and two are not.

questions.question: All the write-skew examples follow the same pattern. What are the three steps?

options.text: A SELECT query checks whether some requirement is satisfied by searching for rows that match some search condition. Depending on the result of the first query, the application code decides how to continue — either to go ahead with the operation, or to report an error and abort. If the application decides to go ahead, it makes a write (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) to the database and commits the transaction
Lock, write, commit
Begin, write, rollback
Read, merge, retry

questions.explanation: The steps may occur in a different order — for example you could first make the write, then the SELECT query, and finally decide whether to abort or commit.

questions.question: Why does the write in step 3 invalidate the check in step 1? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The effect of the write changes the precondition of the decision of step 2 — if you were to repeat the SELECT query from step 1 after committing the write, you would get a different result, because the write changed the set of rows matching the search condition
There is now one fewer doctor on call, or the meeting room is now booked for that time
The position on the board is now taken by the figure that was moved, or the username is now taken
There is now less money in the account

questions.explanation: Five restatements of the same structural fact across the five examples.

questions.question: The doctors example can be made safe with SELECT FOR UPDATE. Why can't the other four?

options.text: Because in the doctors case the row being modified in step 3 was one of the rows returned in step 1, so you can make the transaction safe by locking the rows in step 1. In the other examples the check looks for the absence of rows matching some search condition, and the write adds a row matching the same condition — so if the query in step 1 doesn't return any rows, SELECT FOR UPDATE can't attach locks to anything
Because the other examples involve multiple tables
Because FOR UPDATE is not supported for those queries
Because the other examples are read-only

questions.explanation: You cannot lock rows that don't exist yet — which is exactly the phantom problem.

questions.question: Define a phantom, and what snapshot isolation does about it.

options.text: The effect where a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another transaction is called a phantom. Snapshot isolation avoids phantoms in read-only queries, but in read-write transactions like the examples discussed, phantoms can lead to particularly tricky cases of write skew
A phantom is an aborted write; snapshot isolation removes it entirely
A phantom is a stale read; snapshot isolation prevents it in all transactions
A phantom is a deadlock; snapshot isolation detects it

questions.explanation: Read-only queries are safe; read-write ones are not.

questions.question: Describe the materializing conflicts technique for the meeting room case.

options.text: If the problem of phantoms is that there is no object to which we can attach the locks, perhaps we can artificially introduce a lock object into the database. For the meeting room case you could create a table of time slots and rooms — say 15-minute intervals — with all possible combinations of rooms and time periods created ahead of time, for example for the next six months. A transaction wanting to create a booking can then lock the rows in that table corresponding to the desired room and time period with SELECT FOR UPDATE. The extra table isn't used to store information about the booking; it's purely a collection of locks. The technique is called materializing conflicts because it takes a phantom and turns it into a lock conflict on a concrete set of rows that exist in the database
It creates a trigger that rejects overlapping bookings
It switches to serial execution for booking transactions only
It hashes the room and time into a single key

questions.explanation: Turning a non-existent row into an existing lockable one is the trick.

questions.question: What is the chapter's recommendation about materializing conflicts?

options.text: It can be hard and error-prone to figure out how to materialize conflicts, and it's ugly to let a concurrency control mechanism leak into the application data model — so materializing conflicts should be considered a last resort if no alternative is possible. A serializable isolation level is much preferable in most cases
It is the recommended default approach
It is always preferable to serializable isolation
It should be used whenever phantoms are possible

questions.explanation: Last resort, not first choice.

questions.question: The chapter summarizes why weak isolation is unsatisfying. Which points does it make? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Isolation levels are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented in different databases — for example the meaning of 'repeatable read' varies significantly

If you look at your application code it's difficult to tell whether it is safe to run at a particular isolation level, especially in a large application where you might not be aware of all the things that may be happening concurrently

There are no good tools to help us detect race conditions: static analysis tools may help, but they have not yet found their way into practical use, and testing for concurrency issues is hard because they are usually nondeterministic
The problem is new, having appeared only with distributed databases

questions.explanation: The problem is not new: it has been like this since the 1970s, when weak isolation levels were first introduced — and researchers' answer has always been simple: use serializable isolation.

questions.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee, and what is the strong claim?

options.text: It is usually regarded as the strongest isolation level: it guarantees that even though transactions may execute in parallel, the end result is the same as if they had executed one at a time, serially, without any concurrency. Thus the database prevents all possible race conditions, and if the transactions behave correctly when run individually they continue to be correct when run concurrently
It guarantees only that reads come from a snapshot
It guarantees no aborts will occur
It guarantees writes are durable

questions.explanation: All possible race conditions is an unusually strong claim, which raises the obvious question of why isn't everyone using it — answered by looking at the options for implementing serializability and how they perform.

questions.question: Name the three techniques most databases providing serializability use today.

options.text: Literally executing transactions in a serial order; two-phase locking, which for several decades was the only viable option; and optimistic concurrency control techniques such as serializable snapshot isolation
Quorum reads, version vectors and CRDTs
Snapshot isolation, read committed and read uncommitted
Two-phase commit, consensus and leader election

questions.explanation: The chapter considers these mostly in the context of single-node databases; Chapter 9 examines whether they can be generalized to transactions that involve multiple nodes in a distributed system.

questions.question: Describe actual serial execution and why its isolation is serializable by definition.

options.text: The simplest way of avoiding concurrency problems is to remove the concurrency entirely: to execute only one transaction at a time, in serial order, on a single thread. By doing so we completely sidestep the problem of detecting and preventing conflicts between transactions, and the resulting isolation is by definition serializable
It runs transactions in parallel but commits them in order
It uses one thread per transaction with locking
It batches transactions and applies them atomically

questions.explanation: No concurrency means nothing to reconcile.

questions.question: When did database designers decide a single-threaded execution loop was feasible?

options.text: Around 2007 — even though multi-threaded concurrency was considered essential for getting good performance during the previous 30 years
In 1975, with System R
In 1999, with the SQL/PSM standard
In 2015, with the rise of in-memory databases

questions.explanation: A reversal of 30 years of accepted wisdom.

questions.question: Which developments made single-threaded execution viable? (Select all that apply.)
