options.text: RAM became cheap enough that for many use cases it is now feasible to keep the entire active dataset in memory, so when all data a transaction needs is in memory, transactions can execute much faster than if they have to wait for data to be loaded from disk
Database designers realized that OLTP transactions are usually short and only make a small number of reads and writes
Long-running analytic queries are typically read-only, so they can be run on a consistent snapshot using snapshot isolation, outside of the serial execution loop
CPU clock speeds increased dramatically after 2007

questions.explanation: Clock speeds notably did not increase — that is the trend that made multi-core matter.

questions.question: Which systems execute transactions serially, and what limits the approach?

options.text: VoltDB/H-Store, Redis and Datomic. A single-threaded loop can sometimes perform better than a system that supports concurrency, because it can avoid the coordination overhead of locking — but its throughput is limited to that of a single CPU core, and to make the most of that single thread, transactions need to be structured differently from their traditional form
PostgreSQL and MySQL, limited by disk bandwidth
Cassandra and Riak, limited by network latency
Oracle and SQL Server, limited by memory

questions.explanation: One core is the hard ceiling, which is why partitioning matters here.

questions.question: What did database designers originally intend a transaction to encompass?

options.text: An entire flow of user activity — for an airline booking: searching for routes, fares and available seats; deciding on an itinerary; booking seats on each of the flights of the itinerary; entering passenger details; and making payment. Designers thought it would be neat if that entire process was one transaction so it could be committed atomically
A single row update, as today
A batch of overnight writes
A replication log segment

questions.explanation: The ambition failed because humans are very slow to make up their minds and respond: to support it, databases would need to support a potentially huge number of concurrent transactions, most of them idle, and most databases cannot do that efficiently.

questions.question: What boundary replaced the human-scale transaction on the web?

options.text: Almost all OLTP applications keep transactions short by avoiding interactively waiting for a user within a transaction: on the web, a transaction is committed within the same HTTP request — a transaction does not span multiple requests, and a new HTTP request starts a new transaction
A transaction spans the user's whole session
A transaction spans a day of activity
A transaction spans one TCP connection regardless of requests

questions.explanation: One request, one transaction — humans removed from the critical section.

questions.question: Why does the interactive client/server style make serial execution unusable?

options.text: Because in that style a lot of time is spent in network communication between the application and the database: the application makes a query, reads the result, perhaps makes another query depending on the result, and so on, with statements sent back and forth between the application code on one machine and the database server on another. If you were to disallow concurrency and process only one transaction at a time, the throughput would be dreadful, because the database would spend most of its time waiting for the application to issue the next query — so it is necessary to process multiple transactions concurrently
Because interactive transactions cannot be aborted
Because interactive transactions cannot be logged
Because interactive transactions violate isolation

questions.explanation: Network round-trips would idle the single thread.

questions.question: What do single-threaded systems require instead of interactive transactions?

options.text: They don't allow interactive multi-statement transactions; instead the application must submit the entire transaction code to the database ahead of time, as a stored procedure. Provided all the data needed by the transaction is in memory, the stored procedure can execute very fast without waiting for any network or disk I/O
They require the client to batch all statements in one request without stored procedures
They require the client to hold a lock for the duration
They require the transaction to be split across threads

questions.explanation: Figure 7-9 illustrates the contrast using the doctors-going-off-call example from Figure 7-8.

questions.question: Why do stored procedures have a bad reputation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each database vendor has its own language for stored procedures — Oracle has PL/SQL, SQL Server has T-SQL, PostgreSQL has PL/pgSQL — and these languages haven't kept up with developments in general-purpose programming languages, so they look quite ugly and archaic and lack the ecosystem of libraries you find in most programming languages

Code running in a database is difficult to manage: it is harder to debug, more awkward to keep in version control and deploy, trickier to test, and difficult to integrate with a metrics collection system for monitoring

A database is often much more performance-sensitive than an application server, because a single database instance is often shared by many application servers — so a badly written stored procedure can cause much more trouble than equivalent badly written code in an application server
Stored procedures are not part of any standard

questions.explanation: They have been part of the SQL standard, SQL/PSM, since 1999.

questions.question: Which languages do modern stored-procedure systems use?

options.text: VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic uses Java or Clojure, and Redis uses Lua — modern implementations have abandoned PL/SQL and use existing general-purpose programming languages instead, which is part of why they can achieve quite good throughput on a single thread
All three use PL/SQL
VoltDB uses Lua, Datomic uses Groovy, Redis uses Java
All three use T-SQL

questions.explanation: General-purpose languages plus in-memory data are what made the single thread viable.

questions.question: What else does VoltDB use stored procedures for, and what does that require?

options.text: For replication: instead of copying a transaction's writes from one node to another, it executes the same stored procedure on each replica. This requires that stored procedures are deterministic — they must produce the same result when run on different nodes — so if a transaction needs to use the current date and time, it must do so through special deterministic APIs
For indexing, which requires the procedures be idempotent
For partitioning, which requires the procedures be commutative
For backups, which requires no special property

questions.explanation: Determinism is what lets the procedure itself be the replication log entry.

questions.question: How does partitioning let serial execution scale, and what cross-partition throughput does VoltDB report?

options.text: By partitioning your dataset so that each transaction only needs to read and write data within a single partition, each partition can have its own transaction processing thread running independently — so you can give each CPU core its own partition and let transaction throughput scale linearly with the number of CPU cores. But any transaction that needs to access multiple partitions must be coordinated across all the partitions it touches, performed in lock-step, and such cross-partition transactions are vastly slower: VoltDB reports a throughput of about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second, orders of magnitude below its single-partition throughput, and it cannot be increased by adding more machines
Partitioning has no effect; throughput is always one core
Cross-partition writes reach 100,000 per second
Cross-partition writes scale linearly with machines

questions.explanation: Whether transactions can be single-partition depends on the data: simple key-value data can often be partitioned very easily, but data with multiple secondary indexes is likely to require a lot of cross-partition coordination.

questions.question: Within which constraints is serial execution viable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Every transaction must be small and fast, because it takes only one slow transaction to stall all transaction processing

It is limited to use cases where the active dataset can fit in memory; rarely accessed data could potentially be moved to disk, but if it needed to be accessed in a single-threaded transaction the system would get very slow
Write throughput must be low enough to be handled on a single CPU core, or else transactions need to be partitioned without requiring cross-partition coordination
Cross-partition transactions are possible, but there is a hard limit to the extent to which they can be used

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that if a transaction needs to access data that's not in memory, the best solution may be to abort the transaction, asynchronously fetch the data into memory while continuing to process other transactions, and then restart the transaction — an approach known as anti-caching.

questions.question: For how long was two-phase locking the only widely used serializability algorithm?

options.text: Around 30 years. A footnote notes it is sometimes called strong strict two-phase locking (SS2PL) to distinguish it from other variants of 2PL
Around 10 years
Around 5 years
It has never been widely used

questions.explanation: A boxed warning notes that while two-phase locking (2PL) sounds very similar to two-phase commit (2PC), they are completely different things — 2PC is discussed in Chapter 9.

questions.question: State the two blocking rules that make 2PL's lock requirements much stronger than dirty-write prevention.

options.text: Several transactions are allowed to concurrently read the same object as long as nobody is writing to it, but as soon as anyone wants to write (modify or delete) an object, exclusive access is required. So: if transaction A has read an object and transaction B wants to write to that object, B must wait until A commits or aborts before it can continue — ensuring that B can't change the object unexpectedly behind A's back. And if A has written an object and B wants to read that object, B must wait until A commits or aborts; reading an old version of the object is not acceptable under 2PL
Readers never block writers and writers never block readers
Only writers block writers; readers are always free
Locks are held only for the duration of each statement

questions.explanation: In 2PL writers don't just block other writers; they also block readers and vice versa — the exact inverse of snapshot isolation's mantra, which captures the key difference between them. Because 2PL provides serializability, it protects against all the race conditions discussed earlier, including lost updates and write skew.

questions.question: Which databases use 2PL, and for which isolation level?

options.text: The serializable isolation level in MySQL (InnoDB) and SQL Server, and the repeatable read isolation level in DB2
The read committed level in PostgreSQL and Oracle
The snapshot isolation level in SQL Server only
No mainstream database uses 2PL

questions.explanation: DB2's 'repeatable read' means serializability, which is why it is implemented with 2PL.

questions.question: Describe 2PL's two lock modes and acquisition rules.

options.text: The lock can be in shared mode or exclusive mode. To read an object a transaction must first acquire the lock in shared mode; several transactions are allowed to hold the lock in shared mode simultaneously, but if another transaction already has an exclusive lock on the object they must wait. To write an object a transaction must first acquire the lock in exclusive mode; no other transaction may hold the lock at the same time, either in shared or exclusive mode, so if there is any existing lock on the object the transaction must wait
There is only one mode, exclusive, used for both reads and writes
There are three modes: read, write and intent
Shared locks block each other; exclusive locks do not

questions.explanation: If a transaction first reads and then writes an object it may upgrade its shared lock to an exclusive lock, which behaves the same as getting an exclusive lock directly. Once a transaction has acquired the lock it must continue to hold the lock until the end of the transaction — hence 'two-phase': the first phase, while the transaction is executing, is when the locks are acquired, and the second phase, at the end of the transaction, is when all the locks are released.

questions.question: Define deadlock in the 2PL context, and say who resolves it.

options.text: Because so many locks are in use, it can easily happen that transaction A is stuck waiting for transaction B to release its lock, and vice versa — a situation called deadlock. The database automatically detects deadlocks between transactions and aborts one of them so the others can make progress; the aborted transaction needs to be retried by the application
The application detects deadlocks and the database retries
Deadlocks are impossible under 2PL
Deadlocks resolve themselves after a timeout with no aborts

questions.explanation: Database detects and aborts; application retries.

questions.question: State 2PL's big downside and its causes, in the chapter's order of importance.

options.text: Performance: transaction throughput and response times of queries are significantly worse under two-phase locking than under weak isolation. This is partly due to the overhead of acquiring and releasing all those locks, but more importantly due to reduced concurrency — by design, if two concurrent transactions try to do anything that may in any way result in a race condition, one has to wait for the other to complete
Durability: writes may be lost on deadlock abort
Correctness: 2PL does not actually provide serializability
Complexity: 2PL is hard to implement, but performance is fine

questions.explanation: Reduced concurrency, not lock bookkeeping, is the dominant cost.

questions.question: Why is there no bound on how long a transaction may wait under 2PL?

options.text: Because traditional relational databases don't limit the duration of a transaction, since they are designed for interactive applications that wait for human input — so if one transaction has to wait for another, there is no limit on how long it may have to wait. And keeping your own transactions short isn't sufficient: if several transactions want to access the same object, a queue may form, so a transaction may have to wait for several others to complete before it can do anything
Because transactions have a hard 30-second timeout that is often exceeded
Because deadlock detection is slow
There is a bound; it is the lock timeout

questions.explanation: Unbounded transaction duration plus queueing gives unbounded waits.

questions.question: Describe 2PL's latency behaviour and the operational risk.

options.text: Databases running 2PL can have quite unstable latencies, and they can be very slow at high percentiles if there is contention in the workload — it may take just one slow transaction, or one transaction that accesses a lot of data and acquires many locks, to cause the rest of the system to grind to a halt. This instability is problematic when robust operation is required
Latencies are stable but uniformly high
Latencies are unaffected by contention
Latencies are only affected at the median, not the tail

questions.explanation: Deadlocks can also happen with lock-based read committed isolation, but they occur much more frequently under 2PL serializable isolation — and when a transaction is aborted due to deadlock and retried, it needs to do its work all over again, which can mean significant wasted effort if deadlocks are frequent.

questions.question: What must a serializable database prevent that object locks cannot, and what is the mechanism?

options.text: Phantoms — one transaction changing the results of another transaction's search query. A database with serializable isolation must prevent phantoms, which requires a predicate lock: rather than belonging to a particular object, it belongs to all objects that match some search condition. If transaction A wants to read objects matching some condition it must acquire a shared-mode predicate lock on the conditions of the query, and if transaction B currently has an exclusive lock on any object matching those conditions, A must wait. If A wants to insert, update or delete any object, it must first check whether either the old or the new value matches any existing predicate lock — and if there is a matching predicate lock held by B, A must wait until B has committed or aborted
Deadlocks, prevented by a wait-for graph
Lost updates, prevented by compare-and-set
Dirty reads, prevented by read locks

questions.explanation: For the meeting room example, if one transaction has searched for bookings for a room in a time window, another is not allowed to concurrently insert or update another booking for the same room and time range — but it is okay to concurrently insert bookings for other rooms, or for the same room at a different time.

questions.question: What is 'the key idea' about predicate locks?

options.text: That a predicate lock applies even to objects that do not yet exist in the database, but which might be added in the future (phantoms). If two-phase locking includes predicate locks, the database prevents all forms of write skew and other race conditions, and so its isolation becomes serializable
That predicate locks are cheaper than object locks
That predicate locks never conflict
That predicate locks apply only to existing rows

questions.explanation: Locking the future is what closes the phantom hole.

questions.question: Why are predicate locks replaced in practice, and by what?

options.text: Predicate locks do not perform well: if there are many locks by active transactions, checking for matching locks becomes time-consuming. So most databases with 2PL actually implement index-range locking, also known as next-key locking, which is a simplified approximation of predicate locking. It's safe to simplify a predicate by making it match a greater set of objects — for example a booking for room 123 between noon and 1 p.m. can be approximated by locking bookings for room 123 at any time, or all rooms (not just room 123) between noon and 1 p.m. — because any write that matches the original predicate will definitely also match the approximations
They are replaced by timestamps, which are cheaper
They are replaced by table locks in all cases
They are not replaced; predicate locks are used everywhere

questions.explanation: Over-approximating the predicate is conservative and therefore safe.

questions.question: Where is the range lock attached, and what is the fallback?

options.text: In the booking database there would probably be an index on the room_id column, and/or indexes on start_time and end_time. If the index is on room_id and is used to find existing bookings for room 123, the database can attach a shared lock to that index entry, indicating that a transaction has searched for bookings of room 123; alternatively, if a time-based index is used, it can attach a shared lock to a range of values in that index — say noon to 1 p.m. on January 1, 2018. Either way, an approximation of the search condition is attached to one of the indexes, so any subsequent write that would match the original condition will have to update the same part of the index, encounter the shared lock, and be forced to wait. If there is no suitable index, the database can fall back to a shared lock on the entire table — which will not be good for performance since it will stop all other transactions writing to the table, but it's a safe fallback position
The lock is attached to the row itself; the fallback is a predicate lock
The lock is attached to the transaction; the fallback is abort
The lock is attached to the connection; the fallback is a timeout

questions.explanation: Index-range locks are not as precise as predicate locks — they lock a bigger range of objects than is strictly necessary — but since they have much lower overheads, they are a good compromise.

questions.question: What dilemma does the chapter say it has painted, and what question does it ask?

options.text: That serializable isolation implementations either don't perform well (two-phase locking) or don't scale well (serial execution), while weak isolation levels have good performance but are prone to various race conditions — lost updates, write skew, phantoms and so on. So: are serializable isolation and good performance fundamentally at odds with each other?
That all three approaches perform equally; the question is which to standardize
That weak isolation is always sufficient; the question is why serializability exists
That serializability is impossible; the question is what to use instead

questions.explanation: Which SSI is offered as an answer to.

questions.question: What does serializable snapshot isolation offer, and whose work is it?

options.text: It provides full serializability but has only a small performance penalty compared to snapshot isolation; the chapter calls it very promising. It is fairly new: first described in 2008, and the subject of Michael Cahill's PhD thesis
It provides snapshot isolation only; first described in 1975 by System R
It provides serializability with a large penalty; described by Cahill in 1998
It provides read committed only; described by Härder and Reuter

questions.explanation: It is used in single-node databases — the serializable isolation level in PostgreSQL since version 9.1 — and in distributed databases, with FoundationDB using a similar algorithm. Because SSI is so young compared to other concurrency control mechanisms, it is still proving its performance in practice, but it has the possibility of being fast enough to become the new default in the future.

questions.question: In what sense is 2PL pessimistic, and serial execution 'pessimistic to the extreme'?

options.text: 2PL is a pessimistic concurrency control mechanism: it is based on the principle that if anything might possibly go wrong, it's better to wait until the situation is safe again before doing anything — like mutual exclusion used to protect data structures in multi-threaded programming. Serial execution is pessimistic to the extreme: it is essentially equivalent to each transaction having an exclusive lock on the entire database, or one partition of it, for the duration of the transaction. We compensate for that pessimism by making each transaction very fast to execute, so it only needs to hold the 'lock' for a short time
2PL is optimistic and serial execution is pessimistic
Both are optimistic; SSI is pessimistic
Neither is pessimistic; both are optimistic

questions.explanation: Serial execution is a whole-database lock, made tolerable by short critical sections.

questions.question: Define optimistic concurrency control and the rule about committing.

options.text: Instead of blocking if something potentially dangerous happens, transactions continue anyway in the hope that everything will turn out all right. When a transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether anything bad happened — whether isolation was violated — and if so, the transaction is aborted and has to be retried. Only transactions that executed serializably are allowed to commit
Transactions block on every potential conflict and retry on timeout
Transactions acquire all locks up front and never abort
Transactions run serially but commit optimistically

questions.explanation: Proceed and verify, rather than wait and proceed.

questions.question: Under what conditions does optimistic concurrency control perform badly, and why?

options.text: It performs badly if there is high contention — many transactions trying to access the same objects — as that may lead to a high proportion of transactions needing to abort. If the system is already close to its maximum throughput, the additional transaction load from retried transactions can make performance worse
It performs badly only under low contention
It performs badly only with long-running read-only queries
It always outperforms pessimistic control

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control is an old idea, and its advantages and disadvantages have been debated for a long time. The retry feedback loop is the specific failure mode.

questions.question: Under what conditions does optimistic control win, and what reduces contention?

options.text: If there is enough spare capacity, and if contention between transactions is not too high, optimistic concurrency control techniques tend to perform better than pessimistic ones. Contention can be reduced with commutative atomic operations: for example, if several transactions concurrently want to increment a counter, it doesn't matter in which order the increments are applied, so they can all be applied without conflicting — as long as the counter isn't read in the same transaction
Under high contention, reduced by locking
Under low capacity, reduced by serial execution
Under all conditions, reduced by partitioning

questions.explanation: The caveat on commutativity — not reading the counter in the same transaction — matters.

questions.question: What is SSI built on, and what does it add?

options.text: It is based on snapshot isolation — all reads within a transaction are made from a consistent snapshot of the database — which is the main difference compared to earlier optimistic concurrency control techniques. On top of snapshot isolation, SSI adds an algorithm for detecting serialization conflicts among writes and determining which transactions to abort
It is based on two-phase locking and adds snapshots
It is based on serial execution and adds partitioning
It is based on read committed and adds predicate locks

questions.explanation: Snapshot reads plus conflict detection at commit.

questions.question: Restate the write skew pattern in terms of a 'premise'.

options.text: A transaction reads some data from the database, examines the result of the query, and decides to take some action — a write to the database — based on the result that it saw. Under snapshot isolation the result from the original query may no longer be up to date by the time the transaction commits, because the data may have been modified in the meantime. Put another way, the transaction is taking an action based on a premise — a fact that was true at the beginning of the transaction, for example 'there are currently two doctors on call'. Later, when the transaction wants to commit, the original data may have changed and the premise may no longer be true
A transaction writes first and then reads, invalidating its own write
A transaction reads twice and gets different results
A transaction holds a lock on data it never reads

questions.explanation: Naming the read result a premise is what lets the database reason about it mechanically.

questions.question: Why must the database be conservative about premises?

options.text: Because when the application makes a query, the database doesn't know how the application logic uses the result of that query — to be safe it needs to assume that any change in the query result, the premise, means that writes in that transaction may be invalid. In other words there may be a causal dependency between the queries and the writes in the transaction, so in order to provide serializable isolation the database must detect situations in which a transaction may have acted on an outdated premise and abort the transaction in that case
Because the application always declares its premises explicitly
Because premises are stored in the transaction log
Because the database can infer application logic from the query

questions.explanation: Opacity of application logic is what forces conservatism.

questions.question: Which two cases must the database consider, and what is the timing of each?

options.text: Detecting reads of a stale MVCC object version, where an uncommitted write occurred before the read; and detecting writes that affect prior reads, where the write occurs after the read
Detecting dirty reads and dirty writes, both before the commit
Detecting deadlocks and phantoms, both at commit time
Detecting lost updates and read skew, both after the commit

questions.explanation: The two cases are distinguished by whether the conflicting write precedes or follows the read.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-10 with transactions 42 and 43.

options.text: Snapshot isolation is usually implemented by multi-version concurrency control, and when a transaction reads from a consistent snapshot in an MVCC database it ignores writes that were made by any other transactions that hadn't yet committed at the time the snapshot was taken. Transaction 43 sees Alice as having on_call = true, because transaction 42's modification is uncommitted. However, by the time transaction 43 wants to commit, transaction 42 has already committed — so the write that was ignored when reading from the consistent snapshot has now taken effect, and transaction 43's premise is no longer true. To prevent this anomaly the database needs to track when a transaction ignores another transaction's writes due to MVCC visibility rules, and when the transaction wants to commit it checks whether any of the ignored writes have now been committed; if so, the transaction must be aborted
Transaction 43 sees on_call = false and commits successfully
Transaction 42 aborts and 43 commits with no conflict
Both transactions abort immediately on the stale read

questions.explanation: Track the ignored writes, then check them at commit.

questions.question: Why doesn't SSI abort transaction 43 the moment the stale read is detected? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If transaction 43 was a read-only transaction, it wouldn't need to be aborted, because there is no risk of write skew
At the time when transaction 43 makes its read, the database doesn't yet know whether that transaction is going to later perform a write
Transaction 42 may yet abort or may still be uncommitted at the time when transaction 43 is committed, so the read may turn out not to have been stale after all
Aborting early would violate durability

questions.explanation: By avoiding unnecessary aborts, SSI preserves snapshot isolation's support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

questions.question: For the second case, what mechanism does SSI borrow from 2PL and how does it differ?

options.text: Index-range locks, which lock access to all rows matching some search query such as a shift_id condition — except that SSI locks don't block other transactions. In Figure 7-11, transactions 42 and 43 both search for on-call doctors during shift 1234; if there is an index on shift_id the database can use the index entry 1234 to record the fact that transactions 42 and 43 read this data, and if there is no index this information can be tracked at the table level. This information only needs to be kept for a while: after a transaction has finished — committed or aborted — and all concurrent transactions have finished, the database can forget what data it read
Predicate locks, which do block other transactions
Table locks, held until garbage collection
Row locks, held for the duration of the statement

questions.explanation: Same bookkeeping structure, no blocking behaviour.

questions.question: What must a writing transaction do, and how does the chapter describe the difference from a write lock?

options.text: When a transaction writes to the database it must look in the indexes for any other transactions that have recently read the affected data, and notify them that the data they read may no longer be up to date. This is similar to acquiring a write lock on the affected key range, but rather than blocking until the readers have committed, the lock acts as a tripwire: it simply notifies the transactions that the data they read may no longer be up to date
It must block until all readers have committed, exactly like a write lock
It must abort all readers immediately
It need do nothing; readers check at their own commit time

questions.explanation: A tripwire rather than a barrier — notify, don't block.

questions.question: In Figure 7-11 both transactions notify each other. Which commits and why?

options.text: Transaction 43 notifies transaction 42 that its prior read is outdated, and vice versa. Transaction 42 is first to commit, and it is successful: although transaction 43's write affected 42, 43 hasn't yet committed, so the write has not yet taken effect. However, when transaction 43 wants to commit, the conflicting write from 42 has already been committed, so 43 must abort
Both commit, since neither had committed at the time of notification
Both abort, since each notified the other
Transaction 43 commits and 42 aborts

questions.explanation: Commit ordering decides the winner: whoever commits first wins.

questions.question: What trade-off does the chapter name in SSI's engineering, and what theory does PostgreSQL exploit?

options.text: The granularity at which transactions' reads and writes are tracked: if the database keeps track of each transaction's activity in great detail it can be precise about which transactions need to abort, but the bookkeeping overhead can become significant — less detailed tracking is faster, but may lead to more transactions being aborted than strictly necessary. PostgreSQL exploits the theory that in some cases it's okay for a transaction to read information that was overwritten by another transaction, because it's sometimes possible to prove that the result of the execution is nevertheless serializable — using this to reduce the number of unnecessary aborts
The choice between optimistic and pessimistic locking; PostgreSQL uses 2PL theory
The number of snapshot versions retained; PostgreSQL uses garbage collection theory
The abort timeout; PostgreSQL uses queueing theory

questions.explanation: Precision versus overhead, with a provability escape hatch.

questions.question: Compare SSI with 2PL and with serial execution, and state the constraint the abort rate imposes.

options.text: Versus two-phase locking: a big advantage is that one transaction doesn't need to block waiting for locks held by another transaction — like under snapshot isolation, writers don't block readers and vice versa, which makes query latency much more predictable and less variable, and read-only queries can run on a consistent snapshot without requiring any locks, making SSI very appealing for read-heavy workloads. Versus serial execution: SSI is not limited to the throughput of a single CPU core — FoundationDB distributes the detection of serialization conflicts across multiple machines, allowing it to scale to very high throughput, and even though data may be partitioned across multiple machines transactions can read and write data in multiple partitions while ensuring serializable isolation. The constraint: the rate of aborts significantly affects the overall performance of SSI — a transaction that reads and writes data over a long period of time is likely to run into conflicts and abort, so SSI requires that read-write transactions be fairly short
SSI blocks like 2PL and is limited to one core like serial execution
SSI blocks readers but not writers, and scales to one machine
SSI has no abort rate constraint

questions.explanation: Non-blocking like snapshot isolation, distributable unlike serial execution, but abort-rate sensitive. Long-running read-only transactions may be able to proceed without aborting.

questions.question: Give the summary's definition of what transactions are for.

options.text: Transactions are an abstraction layer that allows an application to pretend that certain concurrency problems and certain kinds of hardware and software faults don't exist — a large class of errors is reduced down to a simple transaction abort, and the application just needs to try again
Transactions are a locking mechanism for protecting shared data
Transactions are a durability guarantee for writes
Transactions are a performance optimization for batched writes

questions.explanation: Errors collapsed into one retryable outcome is the abstraction's payoff.

questions.question: Which applications can manage without transactions, and what do transactions buy the rest?

options.text: Not all applications are susceptible to all those problems: an application with very simple access patterns, such as reading and writing only a single record, can probably manage without transactions. However, for more complex access patterns, transactions can hugely reduce the number of potential error cases you need to think about
Only financial applications need transactions
All applications need transactions equally
Only distributed applications need transactions

questions.explanation: Access-pattern complexity, not data sensitivity, is the criterion.

questions.question: Which error scenarios does the summary name for life without transactions, and what concrete inconsistency?

options.text: Processes crashing, network interruptions, power outages, disk full, unexpected concurrency and more. Without transactions, various error scenarios — processes crashing, network interruptions, power outages, disk full, unexpected concurrency — mean data can become inconsistent in various ways: for example denormalized data can easily go out of sync with the source data, and without transactions it becomes very difficult to reason about the effects that complex interacting accesses can have on the database
Only concurrency problems arise; faults are handled by replication
Only hardware faults arise; concurrency is handled by the application
No inconsistency arises; transactions are purely for convenience

questions.explanation: Denormalized data drifting from its source is the concrete example given.
